Credit Industry Digest
Monday 9 November 2026

Good morning,

Here is your weekly summary of news for credit providers, brokers and financial counsellors.

1. AFCA publishes its latest complaints data
The Australian Financial Complaints Authority has released its quarterly figures on credit-related disputes. Credit reporting remained one of the more common topics, with disputes about listings and repayment history making up a noticeable share. AFCA noted that complaints resolved early, directly between the provider and the consumer, tended to close faster. The full data release is available from AFCA's own website. This item is general industry reporting only.

2. Kestrel Credit Reporting updates its provider guide
Kestrel Credit Reporting has issued a revised guide for providers on supplying repayment history information. The guide clarifies how monthly payment status should be recorded and restates the importance of keeping records of how and when payments are received. Providers are encouraged to review their internal processes against the new wording over the coming months.

3. Hardship practices under the microscope
A roundtable of financial counsellors and lenders discussed how customers first make contact when they are struggling. Participants said the first message is often brief and informal, and that clear, plain-language replies make a real difference to what happens next. Several lenders described changes to their onboarding of hardship requests.

4. Scam and impersonation trends
Industry bodies continue to report lookalike websites and messages imitating credit providers. Providers are reminded to keep customer-facing communications consistent and to publish their official contact channels clearly.

5. Events and training
A series of short webinars on responsible lending and credit reporting obligations begins next month. Registration details are on our events page.

Thank you for reading. If you have a story or event you would like us to consider for a future edition, simply reply to this email and our editorial team will take a look.

About four months ago I got chatting to a man online. He seemed lovely, said he was an engineer working overseas, and we talked every day. After a while he started telling me about a crypto investment he'd been doing really well with, and he said he only wanted to help me set something up so I could have a bit more security in retirement.

He walked me through it over the phone and had me install a program on my computer so he could "help me click through the steps". I didn't really understand it but he was so patient and kind that I just did what he said. He was on my screen for hours some days. The little balance on the investment site kept going up, which made me feel like it was all fine.

Then last month I noticed a $6,000 top-up on my WW Loans personal loan. I never asked for it. I didn't apply for more money and I don't know how it got there. I haven't been able to see where that money went and I'm worried it's gone the same way as everything else. When I tried to ask the man about it he went quiet.

I'm really sorry to bother you with all this. I just didn't know who else to write to. Can someone please get back to me?

Thanks for your patience,
